overview: Gallimimus bullatus was the largest ornithomimosaur known at the time of its description — up to six metres long — from the Late Cretaceous Nemegt Formation of Mongolia. Its long arms, toothless beak, three-toed feet and overall proportions are remarkably similar to a large flightless bird, and it is one of the first dinosaurs demonstrated by trackways to have run at speeds exceeding 40 km/h.

Originally interpreted as a filter-feeder (based on presumed comb-like structures in the beak), Gallimimus is now thought to have been an omnivore, taking insects, small vertebrates and plant material in the manner of a modern cassowary. The Jurassic Park herd stampede scene used Gallimimus as the first large-scale computer-generated dinosaur crowd.

fossilSites.name: Nemegt Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Cretaceous fluvial and aeolian deposits preserving Gallimimus alongside Tarbosaurus, ankylosaurs and giant sauropods.

articles.title: Discovery and description
articles.body: Described by Osmólska, Roniewicz and Barsbold in 1972 from material collected by Polish-Mongolian expeditions in the Gobi Desert. Multiple individuals of different sizes are known. The name means "chicken mimic" referring to superficially bird-like proportions.

articles.title: Locomotion
articles.body: Gallimimus had long, slender hindlimbs with elongate metatarsals — the same configuration seen in fast-running birds. Trackway evidence and muscle-mass estimates suggest running speeds of 40–50 km/h in adults, making it one of the fastest large dinosaurs known. The tail was stiff and horizontal, acting as a counterbalance during locomotion.

articles.title: Diet and behaviour
articles.body: The toothless beak and comparatively small head were originally associated with filter-feeding in water. More recent analyses of jaw mechanics and comparisons with modern omnivorous birds suggest a broader diet of insects, small vertebrates, eggs and plant material. Gallimimus may have formed loose foraging groups similar to ostriches.

fossilRecord.evidence: Long limbs, small head and toothless jaws support ostrich-like locomotion and omnivorous/generalist feeding interpretations.

consensusScope: diet, locomotion and major uncertainty wording

record.mya: early Maastrichtian, roughly 70-68 million years ago
record.description: Gallimimus bullatus was a large, long-limbed ornithomimid from the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia. Multiple partial and nearly complete skeletons, including skulls and juveniles, document a toothless, cursorially specialised biped.
facts: The jaws were toothless and covered by a beak.
Long hindlimbs support efficient running, but a maximum speed cannot be read directly from fossils.
Diet remains unresolved; proposed plant, small-animal and filter-feeding components are hypotheses.

presentation.heroLead: The largest and best-known of the ostrich-like ornithomimids, documented by a series of skeletons from the Gobi that range from young juveniles to adults, yet still without a settled answer to what it ate.

animalParagraphs: Gallimimus was a tall, lightly built theropod from the Nemegt Formation of southern Mongolia. Adults reached about six metres in length, making it the largest ornithomimid known from good material. It had a small head on a long neck, a toothless beak, a compact body and very long hindlimbs with a short thigh and elongated shin and foot.

The skull is low and long-snouted, with large eyes and no teeth at all; the jaws were sheathed in a horny beak. The arms were relatively short compared with other ornithomimids, ending in three-fingered hands whose claws could not be strongly grasped. The tail was long and stiffened towards the tip.

Because its skeleton is known from several individuals at different growth stages, Gallimimus is the reference animal for how ornithomimids were built. Its diet is another matter: the beak has been compared with those of plant-eaters, small-prey hunters and even filter-feeding birds, and the fossils do not yet decide between these ideas.
animalHighlights: A toothless, beaked skull with large eye sockets on a long, slender neck.
Extremely long hindlimbs with elongated shins and feet, the classic build of a fast bipedal runner.
A growth series from small juveniles to adults, unusual for a Cretaceous theropod.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: A keratinous beak with fine ridges is preserved in one specimen, but whether it cropped plants, caught small animals or filtered food from water remains hypothesis.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long shins and feet relative to the thigh are the hallmark of cursorial animals. Actual top speed cannot be read from bones.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Length is well constrained by near-complete skeletons; body mass of roughly 400–500 kg is a model-based estimate.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: No feathers are preserved with Gallimimus itself. A feathered body with bare legs is inferred from Ornithomimus specimens from Canada.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Tsagan Khushu, Nemegt Basin, Ömnögovi Province, Mongolia

locality.name: Tsagan Khushu
locality.note: Nemegt Formation. Specimens were collected by the Polish–Mongolian expeditions of the 1960s and early 1970s and by later Mongolian and international teams across the Nemegt Basin.

presentation.classificationSummary: Gallimimus is an ornithomimid, one of the ostrich-like coelurosaurs. It is usually recovered close to Ornithomimus and Struthiomimus within Ornithomimidae, with the giant Deinocheirus as a more distant relative in Ornithomimosauria.

related.reason: Compare with the North American relative whose specimens preserve feathers.
Compare with a similar-sized ornithomimid known from complete skeletons in Alberta.
Compare with the giant, deep-bodied ornithomimosaur from the same formation.

questions.title: What did it eat?
questions.copy: The toothless beak is compatible with several diets. Ridged structures inside one specimen's beak were compared with the filtering lamellae of ducks, but the comparison is contested and gut contents are unknown.

questions.title: How fast could it run?
questions.copy: Limb proportions suggest a fast runner, and it is often described as ostrich-like in speed, but no published figure is a direct measurement.

questions.title: Do all the referred skeletons belong to one species?
questions.copy: Most Nemegt ornithomimid material has been referred to Gallimimus bullatus. Some specimens differ in details and would benefit from individual reassessment.

review.ageReviewNote: The Nemegt Formation is early Maastrichtian in most current schemes, broadly 70-68 Ma.

evidence.confidenceLimit: Very high for anatomy and bipedality; high for cursorial adaptation; low for exact diet and speed.

panel.headline: Multiple skeletons with skulls, from juveniles to adults.
panel.standfirst: Gallimimus bullatus was named in 1972 from a nearly complete adult skeleton collected by the Polish–Mongolian expeditions. Further skeletons of various sizes from the Nemegt Formation make it one of the best-documented ornithomimosaurs.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Skull, vertebral column, girdles and limbs are all known from more than one individual, including near-complete articulated skeletons and juveniles.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete and near-complete skulls, full vertebral series, pectoral and pelvic girdles, forelimbs with hands and the long hindlimbs and feet, in adults and juveniles. One specimen preserves the keratinous beak.
knownRemains.note: No feathers, skin or gut contents are known for Gallimimus itself, and some referred skeletons have not been individually re-described since the 1970s.

media.title: Mounted holotype skeleton on exhibition
media.alt: Mounted skeleton of Gallimimus bullatus identified as the holotype, photographed on exhibition at Experimentarium, Hellerup, Denmark
media.caption: The skeleton identified as the holotype, ZPAL MgD-I/94, photographed on temporary exhibition in Denmark in 1998. Any missing elements in a mount are reconstructed.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Several complete toothless skulls with lower jaws; one specimen with the keratinous beak preserved.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series with ribs and chevrons in the best skeletons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Scapulocoracoids, three-fingered hands, complete pelvis and the elongated hindlimbs and feet, known in adults and juveniles.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: A keratinous beak with internal ridges in one specimen; no feathers, skin or gut contents.

specimenCards.title: ZPAL MgD-I/94 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A nearly complete adult skeleton with skull collected at Tsagan Khushu by the Polish–Mongolian expeditions and described by Osmólska, Roniewicz and Barsbold in 1972.
specimenCards.meta: Tsagan Khushu · Nemegt Formation · Institute of Paleobiology, Polish Academy of Sciences

specimenCards.title: Juvenile and adult skeletons
specimenCards.description: Additional skeletons of different sizes from the Nemegt Formation, including small juveniles, provide a growth series. A specimen in the Mongolian collections preserves the horny beak that prompted the filter-feeding hypothesis.
specimenCards.meta: Nemegt Basin · Polish and Mongolian collections · some referrals need reassessment

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Complete skulls and skeletons of adults and juveniles, and one preserved beak.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A fast-running, toothless ornithomimid, the largest of its family, whose beak and small head suit an unspecialised or omnivorous diet.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Its actual diet, top speed, the extent and pattern of feathering, and whether every referred skeleton belongs to the same species.
